# On Wandering Without a Destination

I want to write about something that doesn't quite have a name, though people have tried to name it: the experience of thinking without knowing in advance where the thinking will lead. Not argument, which marches toward a conclusion it already half-suspects. Not narrative, which has a shape it's discovering as it goes but still a shape. Something closer to walking through a city you've never visited, where the pleasure is precisely in not knowing which street leads where, and where arriving somewhere specific would almost be a disappointment, a foreclosure of all the other streets you didn't take.

I've been thinking about this because so much of what I do, what anyone does who works with language or ideas, is goal-directed. You write an essay to persuade. You write a story to move someone. You write code to solve a problem. Even play, in our culture, gets justified by its outputs—creativity training, stress relief, bonding. We've become suspicious of activity that doesn't cash out into something. And I wonder if that suspicion has cost us something important, some capacity for genuine openness that can't be faked by pretending to be open while secretly aiming at a target.

Consider the difference between exploring a place and visiting it. When you visit a place, you have a list, even if it's a short one: see the famous bridge, eat at the recommended restaurant, take the photo everyone takes. The place becomes a checklist with scenery. But exploring—real exploring—means letting the place dictate its own terms. You turn left because the light looked interesting, not because anything is there. You sit in a square for forty minutes doing nothing because sitting felt right in that moment. The place reveals itself to you precisely because you've stopped demanding that it perform for you.

I think writing can work the same way, though it's harder to notice because writing always produces an artifact, and artifacts always look like they were aimed at. We retroactively impose intention onto things that may have emerged more accidentally. A writer sits down without knowing what they'll say, follows a phrase because it sounds good, discovers partway through that the phrase was actually about something, follows that thing instead, ends up somewhere they couldn't have predicted at the start—and then, when asked about it later, constructs a story of intention that wasn't really there during the act itself. "I wanted to explore the tension between X and Y." Maybe. Or maybe X and Y only became visible as a tension because you wrote your way into seeing them that way.

This is not a small thing to admit, because intentionality is supposed to be what makes human creation meaningful, what separates it from random noise. If I tell you I didn't know what I was doing, you might reasonably ask why you should care about the result. But I think this gets the relationship between intention and meaning backwards. Meaning doesn't require advance intention; it requires retrospective recognition. You don't need to know where you're going for the going to matter. You need, afterward, to be able to look at where you've been and see that it cohered, that something happened, that the path—however accidental in its turns—added up to a shape worth having traced.

This is actually how most thinking happens, if you're honest about it. The image of the thinker who has a problem, analyzes it methodically, and arrives at a solution is a reconstruction for textbooks. Real thinking is messier. You have a vague itch. You poke at it from a few angles. You get distracted by something adjacent. You come back to the itch with new vocabulary borrowed from the distraction. The vocabulary reshapes the itch into a different question than you started with. You poke at the new question. Eventually something clicks, or doesn't, and you stop—not because you've definitively solved anything but because you're tired, or because the click felt like enough, or because dinner is ready.

There's a kind of fear that attaches to this process, at least for me, which is the fear that wandering will reveal you have nothing inside you worth wandering toward. If you give yourself the freedom to write about whatever you want, with no constraint, no assignment, no deadline forcing a shape—what if what emerges is just thin air? What if the absence of constraint reveals not freedom but emptiness? This fear, I think, is why so many people prefer constraints even when they complain about them. The prompt, the deadline, the genre convention—these all provide a scaffold that absorbs some of the risk. If your sonnet is bad, you can blame the sonnet form for being restrictive. If your free, formless meditation is bad, there's nowhere to hide. You said: here is my mind, unconstrained, doing what it does. And what it does is this.

Maybe that's why open-ended writing feels both liberating and faintly terrifying. It's liberating because nothing is wrong—you cannot fail to hit a target you never set. But it's terrifying for exactly the same reason: there's no external standard to measure against, which means whatever judgment occurs has to come from some internal sense of whether this was worth doing, worth reading, worth the time. And that internal sense is notoriously hard to access honestly. We're so used to outsourcing our judgments—did it get likes, did it get praise, did it fulfill the assignment—that the muscle for self-assessment without external metrics can feel atrophied, or maybe it never developed in the first place.

I want to think about boredom for a second, because boredom is intimately related to this whole topic. Boredom, I suspect, is what happens when you're deprived of external goals and haven't developed the internal capacity to wander productively. A child who hasn't learned to play alone experiences free time as agonizing precisely because nothing is telling them what to do, and they don't yet have the resources to tell themselves. But a child—or an adult—who has cultivated some inner resourcefulness experiences the same free time as spaciousness, as opportunity, as the precondition for genuine discovery rather than the absence of structure. The difference isn't in the external situation, which is identical: unstructured time. The difference is entirely in what capacities you bring to that time.

This makes me think boredom-tolerance, or whatever you want to call the capacity to be productively unoccupied, is actually a kind of skill, maybe even a virtue, and one that's being systematically eroded by a culture of constant stimulation. If every moment of potential boredom gets filled immediately with a phone, a notification, a quick dopamine hit, you never develop the muscle that turns boredom into wandering, wandering into discovery. You just oscillate between stimulation and the discomfort of its absence, never learning that the discomfort, sat with long enough, often transforms into something else—curiosity, attention, even a kind of pleasure that's hard to access any other way.

I don't want to be too precious about this, though, because there's also a way that "the virtue of boredom" becomes its own kind of performance, a humblebrag about how I, unlike the distracted masses, have cultivated deep capacities for unstructured contemplation. That's its own trap. The point isn't to valorize wandering as superior to focus, or unstructured time as superior to goal-directed work. Both have their place. The point is just that wandering has been so devalued, so subordinated to productivity logic, that we've lost some collective sense of how to do it well, and that loss has costs we don't fully register because we've also lost the comparison point that would let us notice what's missing.

Let me try to wander somewhere else now, since I've been wandering around the topic of wandering for a while, which has its own irony I'm aware of but won't belabor.

I think about rivers sometimes, the way a river finds its path not by deciding where to go but by simply following the lowest available gradient at every point, moment to moment, with no overall plan. And yet rivers carve canyons. Rivers create deltas of extraordinary complexity and beauty. The Mississippi River delta, seen from satellite, looks like a living thing, like a nervous system, like something designed by a mind of immense sophistication—and it was made by water doing the simplest possible thing over and over again across geological time: going downhill, locally, repeatedly, without any vision of the whole.

This seems important to me as a model for a different kind of creation than the kind we usually valorize. We tend to think great achievements require great visions—the architect's blueprint, the general's strategy, the CEO's five-year plan. And certainly some achievements do require that. But there's another category of achievement that comes from something more like the river's method: keep making the locally sensible choice, keep following the gradient that's available to you right now, and trust that the larger pattern—if there is to be one—will emerge from the accumulation of those choices rather than from any prior vision imposed on them.

I think a lot of good writing works this way, and a lot of good thinking too. You don't need the blueprint. You need a reasonably good sense of what the next sentence should be, given the sentence before it. If you have that, repeated enough times, with enough attention, something coherent tends to emerge—not always, but often enough that the method is worth trusting. The coherence isn't imposed from above; it's accumulated from below, sentence by sentence, the way the canyon is carved drop by drop.

This is, I realize, a kind of argument for faith—faith in process over faith in vision. And it cuts against a lot of how we're taught to work, especially in contexts that valorize planning, outlining, knowing where you're going before you start. Those approaches aren't wrong, exactly. They work for certain kinds of projects, certain kinds of minds. But they're not the only way, and I sometimes think they get oversold as the only legitimate way, with wandering treated as a failure mode rather than a method in its own right.

There's also something to be said here about control, and our discomfort with relinquishing it. Planning in advance is a form of control: you decide where you're going before you commit to going anywhere. Wandering relinquishes that control, accepts that you don't know, trusts that not-knowing isn't a problem to be solved but a condition to be inhabited. This is hard for a lot of people, myself included on many days, because not-knowing is uncomfortable, especially in a culture that prizes confidence, certainty, the appearance of having things figured out. To wander is to say: I don't have it figured out, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise, and I'm going to proceed anyway.

I want to say something about pleasure here too, because I think wandering, done well, is genuinely pleasurable in a way that's distinct from the pleasure of achievement. Achievement-pleasure is the satisfaction of having gotten somewhere, of the gap between intention and reality closing. It's real, and good, and I don't want to dismiss it. But wandering-pleasure is different. It's the pleasure of the present moment of motion itself, independent of where that motion leads. It's the pleasure a dog has running through a field with no destination, just the pure delight of legs moving and air rushing and smells arriving one after another. Humans can access this pleasure too, but we often suppress it because we've been trained to ask "but what's it for" of every experience, and an experience that has no answer to that question gets devalued, gets treated as lesser, as indulgence rather than as one of the genuine goods available to a creature like us.

I wonder, actually, if the devaluation of purposeless pleasure is connected to a kind of fear—the fear that if we allow ourselves to enjoy things without justification, we'll become undisciplined, unproductive, won't accomplish what we're supposed to accomplish. This fear has some basis; there are people whose lives have been derailed by an excess of unstructured pleasure-seeking with no countervailing discipline. But I think the fear, as a general cultural disposition, is wildly overcalibrated relative to the actual risk. Most people I know don't suffer from too much aimless wandering. They suffer from too little. They suffer from schedules so densely packed with justified activities that there's no room left for the unjustified kind, the kind that doesn't need a reason, the kind that's pursued for no reason other than that, in this moment, it seems like a good idea.

I'm aware that this essay itself is an example of the thing it's describing—I started without a plan, wandered through cities and rivers and childhood boredom and rivers again, and I don't know, even now, near the end, whether this has cohered into anything worth your time. That uncertainty is uncomfortable to sit with, even now, even having just spent two thousand words arguing for the value of sitting with exactly this kind of uncertainty. The argument doesn't make the discomfort disappear. It just gives the discomfort a frame, a context, maybe even a kind of dignity it wouldn't otherwise have.

Maybe that's the most honest thing I can say about wandering: it doesn't eliminate the anxiety of not knowing where you're going. It just asks you to carry that anxiety differently, to treat it as a companion rather than an enemy, to let it ride along with you instead of demanding, before every step, that it be resolved. The destination, if there is one, will arrive or not arrive. In the meantime, there's the walking, the noticing, the turning left because the light looked interesting. There's the next sentence, considered on its own terms, judged only by whether it seems to follow reasonably from the one before. That's not nothing. On certain days, in certain lights, it might even be enough.
